lessons.title: The West Coast offense
lessons.objective: You can say what a West Coast offense actually asks the quarterback to do.

payload.prompt: What is the core idea of the West Coast offense?

options.text: Run the ball relentlessly to set up play-action
Use short, quick, precise passes to do the job a run game usually does
Throw the deep ball on every play to stretch the defense

explanation.correct: The West Coast offense treats short passes like runs. The quarterback gets the ball out fast on timing routes and the receiver runs after the catch, so the passing game moves the chains in small, steady chunks.
explanation.incorrect: Bill Walsh built the West Coast system with the 49ers around fast, precise short passes: a slant, a screen or a checkdown to the back, then yards after the catch.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: That quarterback has West Coast genetics. The ball is out in about two and a half seconds.

payload.question: What is she describing?

options.text: A quarterback who was born on the West Coast
A quarterback trained to release the ball very fast on short routes
A quarterback who only plays in the NFL Western Conference
A quarterback who was drafted by a West Coast team

payload.translation: West Coast genetics means the quarterback was taught to get the ball to receivers on time, before coverage can tighten. A quick, on-schedule release is the goal.

followUps.line: Why would a quick release matter in a West Coast system?
followUps.why: Tests whether you understand that timing routes need precise, fast throws.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: West Coast football is about timing: the receiver breaks just as the ball arrives. That only works if the quarterback throws early and on schedule.

payload.prompt: What does the quarterback do when his first read is covered?
payload.template: If the first read is covered, the quarterback moves to his {{gap1}} read, and the safe last option is a {{gap2}} to the back.

explanation.correct: West Coast quarterbacks work through a quick progression: first read, second, third, then a checkdown. The checkdown is the safety valve that keeps the play alive.
explanation.incorrect: He does not sit and wait. He moves quickly through the progression, and if everyone is covered he checks down to the back for a short, safe gain.

payload.prompt: A West Coast game plan can lean on quick, short passes instead of deep shots. True or false?

scene.alt: A quarterback throwing a quick slant to a receiver near the line.

explanation.correct: True. Quick slants, outs and screens near the line are the heart of the West Coast idea, though deep shots still exist.
explanation.incorrect: Short and quick is the default in a West Coast plan. Deep routes exist, but they are not the core.

payload.prompt: Match the West Coast term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A route where receiver and quarterback share a clock. The ball arrives as the receiver breaks.
A short, safe throw to the running back when the primary reads are covered, keeping the play alive.
The order of receivers the quarterback reads after the snap: first, second, third, then the checkdown.

explanation.summary: Timing routes are the heart of West Coast. Progressions tell the quarterback where to look. Checkdowns are the safety net.

lessons.title: Air Raid and spread
lessons.objective: You can spot Air Raid habits.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Five wide, no huddle, this is pure Air Raid. They are going to throw it all day.

payload.question: What is she identifying?

options.text: The team is about to pass a lot, judging by the formation and tempo
The team will throw exactly 50 passes
This is the West Coast offense
The team is in trouble and desperate

payload.translation: Five wide receivers and no huddle are telltale signs of an Air Raid or spread style. The offense spreads the defense thin and speeds up the tempo, so a lot of passing follows.

followUps.line: Why would no-huddle help a spread offense?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know that no-huddle limits the defense's ability to substitute and adjust.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Air Raid is about spreading the field and playing fast, not hitting a pass count. Volume is the natural result.

payload.prompt: Match the Air Raid term to what it does.

pairs.definition: Several receivers spread wide across the field, stretching the defense sideline to sideline.
Snapping quickly without a huddle so the defense cannot easily substitute or adjust.
A handful of plays practiced endlessly and run from many formations.

explanation.summary: Spread stretches the field. No-huddle limits the defense's adjustments. A few concepts run over and over, from many looks, is the Air Raid recipe: simple for the offense, tiring to defend.

payload.prompt: Why does Air Raid use mostly simple, easy reads?

options.text: Because it is a college-only offense
Because a few concepts, mastered and repeated from many formations, are fast to run and hard to stop
Because defenses cannot figure out simple plays

explanation.correct: Air Raid philosophy says simple and repeated beats clever and rare. The same slant or mesh concept can be dressed up from different formations, and the offense knows it cold and can play fast.
explanation.incorrect: Air Raid is built on a small set of concepts practiced until they are automatic. Good defenses can still stop them, but the offense stays sharp and fast.

payload.prompt: Hurrying up can keep a defense from substituting. True or false?

scene.alt: An offense snapping quickly as the defense tries to sub.

explanation.correct: True. Tempo limits substitutions, so a defense stuck in a pass-first package can be lighter against the run. That is the trap.
explanation.incorrect: Tempo really does limit substitutions and adjustments, which is why offenses use it.

lessons.title: Outside zone and play-action
lessons.objective: You can explain why one play sells the other.

payload.prompt: Put the outside zone and play-action cycle in order.

items.text: Run outside zone again and again
items.why: The back stretches the ball sideways, then plants and cuts upfield where a lane opens.

items.text: Linebackers learn to flow with the stretch
items.why: After a few carries, defenders chase the run fast because they respect it.

items.text: Fake the same outside-zone look with play-action
items.why: The fake looks identical to the run, so the flowing defenders bite.

items.text: Throw behind the linebackers who flowed
items.why: Receivers find space behind them on crossers, deep shots or a bootleg.

explanation.correct: The run builds the trap. Once defenders chase outside zone, the same-looking fake play-action pulls them the wrong way and the throw finds grass behind them.
explanation.incorrect: Start with the run so the defense learns to chase it. Then the same look, but a pass, punishes that chase.

payload.prompt: Why is play-action so effective right after outside zone runs?

options.text: Because the defense is tired
Because linebackers are keyed on the outside-zone stretch and chase it before the fake works
Because the quarterback is a better thrower than runner

explanation.correct: Outside zone trains linebackers to react to the stretch and flow laterally. When play-action shows the same look, some bite, and receivers get space behind them.
explanation.incorrect: The system is built on the defense respecting the run. Run outside zone enough and defenders have to flow with it. Play-action then punishes that instinct with a quick pass or a bootleg.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: That is how the bootleg works. The end crashed on the outside-zone fake, so the quarterback has a mile of space.

payload.question: What did the bootleg accomplish?

options.text: It confused the quarterback
It used the run fake to get the defensive end to chase the wrong way and open space for a pass or scramble
It replaced the running back on the play
It made the defense too tired to stop the next play

payload.translation: A bootleg uses the outside-zone look to pull the defensive end toward the fake. The quarterback then rolls the other way with grass ahead of him and a receiver or two to throw to, or he runs.

followUps.line: Why does the outside-zone run set up a bootleg better than an inside-zone run?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know that outside zone pulls the defense wider.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Run fakes move defenders. The bootleg sends the edge rusher the wrong way and leaves space behind him.

payload.prompt: What does the Shanahan offense need to make outside zone work?

options.text: The defense has to respect the run game enough to pursue it laterally
A very fast running back
The smartest quarterback in the league

explanation.correct: Outside zone works because the defense has to chase the stretch. If defenders stay home and shoot gaps, the run is harder. Respect for the run is what makes the play-action fake work.
explanation.incorrect: It is not about having the fastest back. It is about the defense respecting the run, so that flowing to it leaves space elsewhere.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: That is zone blocking. The guards are working together, and the back is reading the hole, not following a lead blocker.

payload.question: What is the analyst describing?

options.text: Zone blocking: linemen take an area and the back picks the best lane
Zone blocking only works in college
Zone blocking is when everyone blocks the same defender
Zone blocking prevents holding penalties

payload.translation: Zone blocking is the Shanahan staple. Linemen block an area, working together, instead of each having one assigned defender. The back reads which blocker has the advantage and cuts there. Gap or man-style blocking gives each lineman a specific target instead.

followUps.line: Is that inside zone or outside zone?
followUps.why: Both use zone blocking. Outside zone stretches wide; inside zone attacks closer to the middle.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Zone blocking is linemen saying 'I have this area' and the back picking the lane. Ask which run scheme it is, not just the word.

lessons.title: Motion tells
lessons.objective: You can use motion to guess man or zone.

statement.speaker: Quarterback
statement.text: Before the snap, I motion my receiver across the formation. The corner follows him. That tells me it is man coverage.

payload.question: How does the motion tell him it is man?

options.text: In man coverage, a defender shadows one player everywhere he goes
The corner is just being friendly
Motion always reveals coverage
The corner is confused by the motion

payload.translation: When a receiver motions across the formation, he tests the defense. A defender following him is a strong hint of man coverage. A defender who stays in his area suggests zone. It is a clue, not a guarantee, because defenses disguise.

followUps.line: What would happen if it were zone coverage and the receiver motioned?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know the defender would stay in place, not follow.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Motion is a clue. A corner who follows usually means man; one who stays usually means zone. Say 'looks like' rather than 'definitely.'

payload.prompt: Why do offenses use motion before the snap?

options.text: To confuse the defense into penalties
To read the coverage and find weak spots
Because it is fun to move around

explanation.correct: Motion is information. The quarterback watches who follows the motion, which often hints at man or zone, and how the defense shifts. That informs the read.
explanation.incorrect: Before the snap, offenses move a receiver or back. The defense's reaction tells the quarterback what to expect, though good defenses can disguise it.

statement.speaker: Safety
statement.text: After the motion, I slid over so the corner had help deep.

payload.question: What did the safety just do?

options.text: He was confused by the motion
He shifted his deep help toward where the offense showed strength
He left the deep middle open on purpose for a blitz
He is required to follow the motion man

payload.translation: Defenses adjust to motion. A safety shifting his deep help to the stronger side is a rotation, a way to change the look or stay balanced. Zone-based coverage adjusts like this, but it is not a perfect tell.

followUps.line: Did that change the coverage, or just the shell?
followUps.why: Good question: a rotation can change the look or the coverage itself, and defenses use it to disguise.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Safety movement is a clue, never a guarantee. Ask what changed rather than announcing what coverage it was.

payload.prompt: What else can motion reveal besides man or zone?

options.text: How many defenders are in the box, which tells you if the defense is ready to stop the run
The color of the defense's jerseys
Whether the defense is happy or sad

explanation.correct: A defender who follows motion out of the box leaves a lighter box. A light box invites a run; a loaded box (eight or more near the line) invites a pass. Motion is one way to see which one you have.
explanation.incorrect: Motioning a running back wide and watching whether a linebacker follows shows the quarterback how many defenders are really near the line, which shapes the play call.

lessons.title: Match and disguise
lessons.objective: You can explain why coverage names are slippery.

payload.prompt: What is match coverage?

options.text: A coverage that starts like zone but turns into man once receivers enter the coverage area
A coverage where everyone plays man coverage
A coverage where everyone plays zone coverage

explanation.correct: Match coverage is a hybrid. It looks like zone before the snap, but once a receiver enters a defender's area, that defender matches him like man coverage. That makes it hard to read.
explanation.incorrect: Modern defenses are rarely pure. Match coverage starts with zone rules and matches routes as they develop.

payload.prompt: You call match coverage but show a Cover 2 look. What do you gain?

situation.narrative: The offense is running a route combination designed to beat Cover 2. You want to show them Cover 2 pre-snap, but you have match coverage that can adjust when routes develop.

facts.label: Offensive read
facts.value: Routes designed to hit seams in Cover 2

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: Match looks like Cover 2 but adapts post-snap

options.label: Disguise match as Cover 2 and let them run into it
options.consequence: The offense sees two safeties and throws to the seam. But your zone defender has already matched the tight end or running back man-to-man. The throw is incomplete or intercepted.
considerations: They see Cover 2 but get something else

options.label: Just play pure Cover 2
options.consequence: You show what you are. The offense runs the exact seam route designed to beat Cover 2. They complete it and gain 15 yards.
considerations: Disguise is worth more than honesty

payload.expertNote: Modern defenses win with disguise. Showing one coverage and playing another lets the defense react to what happens, not just what the offense planned.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: It looked like Cover 2 before the snap, but it played like Cover 3 after. A linebacker matched the running back.

payload.question: Why is the coverage name confusing?

options.text: The analyst is wrong about what coverage it was
Modern defenses mix and match so much that the name becomes slippery and depends on post-snap action
Cover 2 and Cover 3 are the same thing
The defense is breaking the rules

payload.translation: Coverage names describe what the defense shows and does. Match and hybrid coverages blur that, because they can look like one thing pre-snap and play like another. That is why announcers sometimes disagree about the name.

followUps.line: Is it still Cover 2 if it changes after the snap?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know coverage is fluid, not fixed.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Coverage names are slippery by design. 'Looked like Cover 2, played like Cover 3' is an honest thing to say.

payload.prompt: Match coverage can look like zone before the snap and play like man after it.

scene.alt: A defense showing two deep safeties before the snap.

explanation.correct: True. A zone-looking shell hides the plan, and once routes develop the defenders match them. The offense cannot key on a single tell.
explanation.incorrect: It really is both. The zone look hides intentions; matching receivers after the snap gives man-style tightness.

lessons.title: Tampa 2 and zone blitz
lessons.objective: You can describe two classic defensive ideas.

payload.prompt: Match the defensive concept to what it does.

pairs.definition: Cover 2 with the middle linebacker dropping deep into the middle, making three deep defenders.
A lineman drops into coverage while a linebacker or defensive back rushes, muddling blocking assignments.
Two safeties each take half of the deep field; corners cover the flats.

explanation.summary: Cover 2 is the base, Tampa 2 adds a deep middle linebacker, and the zone blitz hides who rushes and who drops. All three are about hiding what the defense is doing until after the snap.

payload.prompt: Tampa 2 is named for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, who made it famous.

scene.alt: A Cover 2 shell with the middle linebacker dropping into the deep middle.

explanation.correct: True. Coaches Tony Dungy and Monte Kiffin used it with Tampa Bay in the late 1990s and early 2000s, and it became a signature look across the league.
explanation.incorrect: Tampa 2 really is named for Tampa Bay, where the Buccaneers built a strong defense around it.

statement.speaker: Offensive Coordinator
statement.text: They are showing a four-man rush but it is a zone blitz. The end is dropping, and the linebacker is coming up the middle.

payload.question: Why is this deception a problem?

options.text: The offensive line is expecting a four-man rush from the line and gets fooled when a linebacker comes free
The zone blitz is illegal
The offense cannot run the ball on this play
The quarterback is required to throw the ball instantly

payload.translation: Zone blitz is a misdirection. The line blocks the four guys they see, but one of them is dropping back. Meanwhile, a linebacker or safety comes up the middle or the edge unblocked. The free rusher is devastating because nobody planned to stop him.

followUps.line: How would the offense stop a free rusher from a zone blitz?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know the offense needs a hot route or check to pick up the unblocked rusher.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Zone blitz wins by creating a free rusher through disguise rather than extra numbers.

payload.prompt: What does Tampa 2 add to regular Cover 2?
payload.template: Tampa 2 adds a {{gap1}} linebacker who drops into the deep {{gap2}}, making three deep defenders.

explanation.correct: Regular Cover 2 leaves a hole in the deep middle between the two safeties. In Tampa 2 the Mike linebacker drops there, which takes away seam and dig routes.
explanation.incorrect: The fix for Cover 2's middle hole is the middle linebacker dropping deep. The cost is one fewer defender near the run.

lessons.title: Boxes and mismatches
lessons.objective: You can say why the box count and mismatches drive play calls.

payload.prompt: Six defenders are in the box with one safety deep. Run or pass?

situation.narrative: It is second and eight. One safety is deep. Six defenders are near the line of scrimmage.

options.label: Run the ball
options.consequence: A light box gives the blockers the numbers. Your back finds a crease and gains five or six, setting up third and short.
considerations: Six defenders in the box is a light box
Third and short keeps the whole playbook open

options.label: Throw it to a receiver
options.consequence: One safety over the top gives a decent one-on-one chance, but you passed up a favorable run look and risk an incompletion.
considerations: But incompletions stop the clock and waste the numbers
The run look is the better gift

payload.expertNote: A light box invites the run, because you have more blockers than they have box defenders. A loaded box (eight or more) does the opposite and invites a pass. Take the gift the defense offers.

statement.speaker: Quarterback
statement.text: Their linebacker is covering our slot receiver. That is a mismatch. We are going to abuse that all day.

payload.question: Why does he want to throw to the slot?

options.text: The linebacker is bigger and will fall down
The receiver is faster and more agile than the linebacker, creating an advantage
Slot receivers always beat linebackers
The quarterback is tired of running plays

payload.translation: A mismatch is when a receiver faces a defender who is not built to cover him, like a fast slot receiver on a linebacker. The quarterback attacks it.

followUps.line: How does a defense create the mismatch it wants the offense to attack?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know defenses sometimes invite bad matchups to get rush pressure.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Mismatch is about fit, not talent. A linebacker covering a slot receiver is a mismatch because covering space is not his job.

payload.prompt: What does a quarterback read when he counts the box?

options.text: Whether the defense can stop the run, which helps him choose between run and pass
How much the defense loves him
What the weather is going to be

explanation.correct: The quarterback counts defenders inside the box, roughly tackle to tackle near the line. Around seven is normal. Eight or more is a loaded box: tougher to run, so throw. Six or fewer is a light box: good to run.
explanation.incorrect: Box count is a pre-snap read. More defenders than blockers, throw. More blockers than defenders, run.

statement.speaker: Safety
statement.text: We are in a single-high shell. I am one-on-one with their number-one receiver. Best of luck to me.

payload.question: What is the safety worried about?

options.text: The defense has no help over the top so he is vulnerable to deep throws
The weather is bad
The receiver is shorter than him
The field is wet

payload.translation: Single-high means one safety deep and no help. The corners and receivers are on islands. A deep pass to a great receiver in one-on-one coverage is a coin flip. The offense likes this, especially with speed or height advantages.

followUps.line: Why would a defense show single-high if it is so dangerous?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know defenses sacrifice some coverage to stop the run.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Single-high is a gamble. You get better run defense and less yardage to the first down, but you lose deep safety help. One-on-one corners can lose. Elite receivers win that coin flip.
